title: Rise Brewing v. PepsiCo
backgroundAndFacts:
RiseandShine Corporation, doing business as Rise Brewing, is a small company that sells canned coffee drinks under the brand name 'RISE.' PepsiCo, one of the world's largest beverage companies, launched a line of energy drinks also called 'RISE.' Rise Brewing sued PepsiCo for trademark infringement, arguing that consumers would confuse the two brands and that PepsiCo was trading off the goodwill Rise Brewing had built in its mark.

The central legal dispute is not merely about whether consumers might mix up the two products, but about when and by whom that confusion must occur. Rise Brewing argued, among other theories, that even if a buyer at the moment of purchase is not confused, third parties who later see the product—say, a friend seeing someone drink PepsiCo's RISE energy drink—might be confused and think it was Rise Brewing's product. This is known as 'post-sale confusion.' The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit ruled against Rise Brewing, and the company asked the Supreme Court to weigh in.

The Supreme Court agreed to hear the case in June 2026. The United States government, through the Solicitor General, filed a brief supporting vacating the lower court's decision, and numerous intellectual property organizations filed amicus briefs, reflecting how broadly this case is expected to affect trademark law across many industries.
legalQuestion: Whether a trademark owner asserting a likelihood of confusion must demonstrate that consumers are likely to be confused at the time of purchase, or whether post-sale confusion—confusion experienced by third-party observers after the sale is complete—is sufficient to support a trademark infringement claim.
significance:
This case could reshape the boundaries of trademark law by clarifying whether companies can use the theory of 'post-sale confusion'—confusion among bystanders who see a product after it has been purchased—to win infringement claims. If post-sale confusion alone is sufficient, trademark rights become substantially broader, potentially allowing large brand owners to block competitors even when buyers themselves are not confused at the point of sale. Critics argue this could give established brands excessive power to suppress competition.

For small businesses and startups, the outcome matters enormously: a ruling that limits post-sale confusion could make it harder to fend off larger competitors who adopt similar-sounding names. Conversely, narrowing post-sale confusion could protect newer companies from overreaching infringement claims by incumbent brands. The case has attracted attention from trademark scholars, the U.S. government, and multiple major intellectual property associations, signaling its potential to reset standards applied in trademark disputes nationwide.

parties.coreArgument: Rise Brewing argues that the Second Circuit applied an improperly narrow view of trademark confusion by failing to adequately credit post-sale confusion and other recognized theories of consumer confusion. Trademark law has long protected brand owners from confusion that occurs not only at the point of sale but also after purchase, when third-party observers may be misled about the source of a product.
supportingPoints: Post-sale confusion is a well-established and legitimate theory under the Lanham Act that courts have recognized for decades.
The Second Circuit's analysis improperly discounted evidence that bystanders and non-purchasing consumers could be confused between RISE Brewing and PepsiCo's RISE energy drink.

Allowing a massive corporation like PepsiCo to adopt a mark nearly identical to a small, established brand undermines the core purpose of trademark law, which is to protect consumers and brand owners alike.
The lower court's ruling creates a circuit conflict and uncertainty about what forms of consumer confusion support a viable infringement claim.

parties.coreArgument: PepsiCo argues that the Second Circuit correctly found no actionable likelihood of confusion, and that post-sale confusion theories should not be stretched to cover situations where sophisticated buyers at the point of sale are not actually confused. Expanding post-sale confusion would give trademark holders an unwarranted monopoly over common words and unfairly restrict legitimate competition.
supportingPoints: The two products occupy different market segments—canned coffee versus energy drinks—and are sold through different channels, reducing any realistic likelihood of confusion.
Trademark law's primary concern is protecting consumers from deception at the point of purchase; extending liability based on speculative bystander confusion goes beyond the statute's purpose.
Allowing broad post-sale confusion theories would chill competition by enabling brand owners to monopolize descriptive or common terms like 'RISE.'
The record supports the lower court's factual findings, and there is no genuine circuit split requiring Supreme Court intervention.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Qualitex Co. v. Jacobson Products Co.
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: Cited for the broad purposes of trademark law under the Lanham Act, including protecting against consumer confusion and ensuring that marks serve as reliable indicators of source.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Two Pesos, Inc. v. Taco Cabana, Inc.
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: Cited for the principle that inherently distinctive trade dress is protectable under the Lanham Act without proof of secondary meaning, relevant to the breadth of trademark protection.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Polaroid Corp. v. Polarad Electronics Corp.
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: The Second Circuit's multi-factor likelihood-of-confusion test from this case governs how courts in that circuit evaluate whether two marks are likely to confuse consumers, and its application is central to the dispute.
Cited as the Ninth Circuit's analogous multi-factor likelihood-of-confusion framework, relevant to arguments about circuit approaches to post-sale confusion.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Lois Sportswear, U.S.A., Inc. v. Levi Strauss & Co.
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: One of the foundational Second Circuit cases recognizing post-sale confusion as a valid theory of trademark infringement, cited in the debate over whether that doctrine was correctly applied below.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Gruner + Jahr USA Publishing v. Meredith Corp.
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: Cited for the proposition that the likelihood-of-confusion analysis must be flexible and attentive to the context in which confusion occurs, supporting Rise Brewing's argument for a broader confusion inquiry.
